newsitem.title: UK: UK think-tank wants curb on arms to Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: UK think-tank wants curb on arms to Indonesia.

text.p: An independent foreign affairs think-tank on Friday called for strict curbs on the sale of British arms to Indonesia, saying there were clear signs they would be used to suppress internal protests.
Saferworld called on the new Labour government to stick to its promise that from now on British foreign policy would revolve around human rights.

"Indonesia is a test case for Britain's new foreign policy. The British government should be quite clear that it will not furnish dictatorial regimes with their tools of repression," Saferworld executive director Paul Eavis said in a statement.
Human rights activists accuse the Indonesian government of gross violations and say up to 200,000 people have died in the former Portuguese colony of East Timor since Jakarta sent in troops in 1975.
Protest groups here say there is clear evidence that British-made jet fighters, armoured personnel carriers and water cannon have been used to quell protests in Indonesia.
Indonesia says criticism of its human rights record is unfounded.
Saferworld said it was likely that British equipment would be used to deal with any protests at the forthcoming May 29 election in Indonesia.
Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said earlier this week that applications for export licences to sensitive states would be examined very closely.

Saferworld said export licences should not be granted for equipment which might be used for internal repression and should also be denied unless the recipients could prove the arms were legitimately needed for defence reasons.

It said all licence applications for the export of armoured personnel vehicles, water cannon, riot equipment and small arms to Indonesia should be refused, a stance which had been adopted by the United States.
Saferworld also called for an inquiry to examine repeated reports that British Aerospace Hawk jets had been used for internal repression. The company denies the charges.

Last month the European parliament reiterated its demands for the Jakarta authorities to "end torture and executions", and called on EU states to stop all military assistance and arms sales to Indonesia.
In December 1996 East Timorese Nobel peace prize laureate Ramos Horta accused Britain of being the "greatest arms smuggler" to Indonesia.
